findings.claim: A CLD should focus on 'the core system engine (two or three loops)'
findings.failure_mode: Core system engine is a set of central nodes/variables around which loops focus; no 'two or three loops' figure in the source
findings.fix: correct: the core system engine (the one or handful of central variables) and the feedbacks around it

findings.claim: Rich Pictures are 'particularly useful when safety is low'
findings.failure_mode: Source names power dynamics as a Rich Pictures weakness: dominant individuals can force the group to draw only their view, and 'others may be too nervous or fearful to contribute'; it gives no low-safety advantage
findings.fix: strip 'particularly useful when safety is low'; keep the diverse-roles clause

findings.claim: 'feedback-structural analysis is what a fifth-Whys pass cannot produce'
findings.failure_mode: Claim about Five Whys; the source never mentions Five Whys (no match in converted text) and the deep ref makes no comparison
findings.evidence: Deep ref has no Five Whys content; source grep 'five whys' = 0 hits
findings.fix: strip

findings.claim: "Rich Pictures are a drawing, a picture, of a system or 'situation.' Very few, if any, prompts are given by facilitators beyond asking them to 'draw the system.'"
findings.failure_mode: Two non-contiguous source sentences stitched into one quotation without ellipsis, 'very' recapitalised; no [V] marker
findings.fix: re-mark: [V] and split into two quotations or insert '...'

findings.claim: Strengths include "flexibility, openness, ability to capture different perspectives/values/perceptions, low barrier to participation."
findings.failure_mode: The deep ref's own paraphrase list is put in quotation marks as if the authors' words; the only [V] in that deep-ref passage is 'even in a tricky process... there is still something to work with'
findings.fix: correct: remove quotation marks (paraphrase), or quote the [V] fragment 'even in a tricky process... there is still something to work with'

findings.claim: A CLD surfaces feedback structure 'something a Five Whys pass, which follows a linear causal chain, cannot reach' (Ch 4)
findings.failure_mode: Premise about another method inserted into a Ch 4-cited concept; nothing in the deep ref or source about Five Whys
findings.evidence: Deep 115-127; source has no Five Whys
findings.fix: strip the Five Whys clause

findings.claim: A CLD is "usually focused around a 'core system engine' — a set of nodes at the centre of the system."
findings.failure_mode: Quotation is not verbatim (source: 'The feedback loops are usually focused around a core system engine, which is a set of nodes that are the core of the system'); subject changed from 'the feedback loops' to 'a CLD'; no marker
findings.fix: correct: "The feedback loops are usually focused around a 'core system engine', which is a set of nodes that are the core of the system" [V]

findings.claim: Participatory maps become "boundary objects around which stakeholders and researchers can learn" (citing Star & Griesemer, 1989)
findings.failure_mode: Quotation silently elides '(see Star & Griesemer, 1989)' from inside the quoted span; no [V]/[BT] marker
findings.fix: re-mark: 'boundary objects' ... "around which stakeholders and researchers can learn" [V] [BT]

findings.claim: "when working in a genuine complex adaptive system, it is highly unlikely we will have access to the breadth or depth of quantitative data or evidence we need." [V]
findings.failure_mode: Truncated mid-sentence without ellipsis, which broadens the claim: the source says the data 'we need to formally validate every node and edge in a system map'
findings.fix: correct: "...quantitative data or evidence we need to formally validate every node and edge in a system map" [V]

findings.claim: When 'safety is low or dominant voices are shaping the data-gathering phase', use Rich Pictures with leave-the-room facilitation: 'The drawing surfaces what verbal input suppresses when someone powerful is watching.' (Ch 2, Common Issues)
findings.failure_mode: Inverts the cited section. Ch 2 names dominant individuals as a Rich Pictures problem ('Individuals can force a group to draw only their view, or others may be too nervous or fearful to contribute') and says power dynamics 'can only be done in the planning and inviting stages'. Leaving the room is about the facilitator handing over their own power, not countering a dominant participant
findings.fix: correct: If a dominant voice is likely, manage it at planning and inviting (separate groups or sessions; Ch 2, "Common Issues and 'Tricks of the Trade'"; Ch 10, 'Common Issues'); during drawing, the facilitator gives away their own power by leaving the room

findings.claim: 'Keep the first draft small — five to eight variables.' (Ch 4, 'How Do You Create Causal Loop Diagrams?')
findings.failure_mode: Figure not in the source and cited to a step that says the first diagram is the core engine plus about twenty nodes; also inconsistent with the distillation's own Concept 6 ('twenty nodes maximum')
findings.fix: correct: Build the first diagram around the engine, up to about twenty nodes ('Twenty nodes seem to be a useful limit here' [V])

findings.claim: 'Use the submap to identify where an intervention would have the most structural leverage.' (Ch 5)
findings.failure_mode: Submaps focus on 'particular questions or issues'; the source does not frame them as leverage finders (the closest Ch 5 notion is an influential, controllable 'system lever', not in the deep ref)
findings.fix: correct: Use the submap to see what drives this factor and what it drives

findings.claim: Horrendogram response: 'Trim the rest. A smaller, sharper map is more useful than a complete one.' (Ch 4, "Commons Issues and 'Tricks of the Trade'")
findings.failure_mode: The cited trick says the opposite: 'The point should not be to just produce a very simple map ... but to also think carefully about how you might frame and introduce it in ways which allow you to keep as much complexity as possible (e.g. introduce it in steps...)'. PSM's answer to horrendograms is likewise 'without compromising on depth'
findings.fix: correct: Refocus on the core system engine and introduce the rest in steps (colour-code or group by theme) rather than deleting it; for a large map, work through submaps

findings.claim: 'Is this problem genuinely complex (feedback structure, time delays, multi-stakeholder)? If it is a simple, one-off issue, a Five Whys pass is the right tool. CLDs are overhead on simple problems.' (Ch 11)
findings.failure_mode: Ch 11 does not mention Five Whys; the complexity checklist (time delays, multi-stakeholder) is SSDL Brief 1.02's list, attributed here to Ch 11. The supportable part is Ch 4's 'if feedback loops are not present, or important, in your system, then the method will be less useful'
findings.evidence: Deep 127, 283-289; ssdl-systems-thinking-foundations-deep 55; source has no Five Whys
findings.fix: correct: Are feedback loops present and important here? If not, a CLD 'will be less useful' (Ch 4, 'What Are Causal Loop Diagrams Good and Bad At?'); strip the Five Whys recommendation

findings.claim: 'If it targets a symptom rather than a loop, the loop will compensate when the experiment ends.' (Ch 4, 'What Is a Causal Loop Diagram?')
findings.failure_mode: Causal claim not in the deep ref or source, cited to Ch 4
findings.fix: correct: Does the experiment disrupt the vicious cycle or only one of its symptoms? (Ch 4, "Commons Issues and 'Tricks of the Trade'")

findings.claim: Prioritise experiments that address 'factors with the most connections or the most structurally central position. Favour interventions on the core system engine over those on peripheral nodes.' (Ch 4)
findings.failure_mode: Prioritisation rule not in the deep ref; Ch 4 describes the engine as the map's focus but does not rank interventions by centrality
findings.fix: correct: Which experiment would disrupt a vicious cycle or strengthen a virtuous one in the CLD? (Ch 4)

findings.claim: Diagnosis: 'A feedback structure is keeping the problem in place; Five Whys cannot reach it'
findings.failure_mode: Five Whys premise not in the source (as D003, D006)
findings.fix: correct: A feedback structure may be keeping the problem in place

findings.claim: 'Safety is low and dominant voices are shaping data gathering — the leave-the-room facilitation move for Rich Pictures is the structural counter.'
findings.failure_mode: Same inversion as D010: the source says dominant individuals can take over a Rich Picture and power dynamics can only be managed at planning and inviting
findings.fix: strip

findings.claim: 'Apply the appropriateness triangle first: is this problem genuinely complex (feedback structure, time delays, multi-stakeholder)? If not, a shorter diagnostic pass is the right tool' (Ch 11)
findings.failure_mode: Recasts the triangle (project purpose/constraints x system characteristics x method nature, for choosing among methods) as a complexity checklist; checklist items come from SSDL Brief 1.02
findings.fix: correct: Apply the appropriateness triangle: do the project's purpose and constraints and the system's characteristics fit a CLD? If feedbacks are not important, a CLD 'will be less useful' (Ch 4)

findings.claim: The facilitator applies the appropriateness triangle (multi-stakeholder, time delays, recurring pattern) and 'The team meets the threshold for a CLD.'
findings.failure_mode: The triangle has no threshold and is not a complexity checklist; the example checks only system characteristics and skips the project-purpose and method-nature corners
findings.fix: correct: add the project corner (a 90-minute retro, the team's visual literacy) and the method corner (CLDs suit systems where feedbacks matter), then conclude a CLD fits

findings.claim: 'Three sub-groups of two draw their picture'
findings.failure_mode: Group size conflicts with the source guidance the example cites (smaller groups of three to six per picture) and with the distillation's own Concept 4
findings.fix: correct: two sub-groups of three

findings.claim: 'The appropriateness triangle, Rich Picture facilitation, horrendogram warning, boundary-object redirect, and ToC structure are all from Barbrook-Johnson & Penn (Ch 2 ...; Ch 3 ... [V]; Ch 4 ... [V]; Ch 11 ... [V])'
findings.failure_mode: [V] attached to bare section citations with no quoted text; the example does not actually use a horrendogram warning or boundary-object redirect; no verbatim blockquote is included
findings.fix: correct: drop [V] from citations; list only concepts the example uses; add one [V] blockquote from the deep ref (e.g. the appropriateness definition, deep 285)

findings.claim: 'Using Five Whys to analyse a problem that has a feedback structure — linear causal chains do not reach feedback loops, so the root cause identified will be a symptom of the loop'
findings.failure_mode: Five Whys claim not in source; presented as an anti-pattern this reference helps avoid
findings.fix: strip

findings.claim: 'Introducing CLD or archetype thinking before the team's own analysis has stalled, reinforcing a facilitator-as-expert dynamic'
findings.failure_mode: This is SSDL Brief 1.07's warning (archetypes can 'reinforce a dynamic of expert vs. novice'), presented as this reference's. Barbrook-Johnson & Penn recommend archetypes as core-engine seeds; their related point is that CLDs put 'a lot of power in the researcher's hands'
findings.fix: correct: Letting the facilitator hold the pen on a CLD, which puts a lot of power in the researcher's hands (Ch 4); for the archetype-timing warning, cite SSDL Brief 1.07

findings.claim: OT: 'When the CLD's core system engine is a structural constraint (team archetype mismatch), OT vocabulary names the escalation path'
findings.failure_mode: OT has no 'escalation path'; its mismatch is strategy-vs-design misfit (ASSESS), and its change path is the MADE method's DESIGN and ELEVATE steps
findings.fix: correct: ...OT's ASSESS step names the strategy-design mismatch and DESIGN/ELEVATE give the change path

findings.claim: FLO 'names' the leave-the-room move 'as giving power to participants'; complementary on low-safety data gathering
findings.failure_mode: The FLO deep ref contains no leave-the-room or give-power move; 'give power to the participants' is Barbrook-Johnson & Penn's own Ch 2 trick. FLO's nearest idea is facilitators stepping back as an online course matures (scaffolding-then-fading)
findings.fix: correct: FLO's scaffolding-then-fading arc (facilitators 'step back' as the group develops) parallels this source's 'give power to the participants' trick

findings.claim: Psychology 2e 'explains why Rich Pictures surface data that stickies suppress (conformity, normative social influence)'
findings.failure_mode: Premise not in either source: Barbrook-Johnson & Penn never compare Rich Pictures with sticky notes and name group dominance as a Rich Pictures weakness; Psychology 2e covers conformity but not this application
findings.fix: correct: Psychology 2e's conformity research (Asch; normative social influence) explains the dominance risk this source names for Rich Pictures and why power dynamics must be managed at planning

findings.claim: 'None of Meadows, Star & Griesemer, or Sterman are held directly in this corpus; this distillation does not cite them.'
findings.failure_mode: Self-contradiction: line 28 cites Star & Griesemer (1989)
findings.fix: correct: ...this distillation cites Star & Griesemer only as the source of the boundary-object term (borrowed-through)

findings.claim: The book 'does not cover mind mapping, stakeholder mapping, social network analysis, path analysis'
findings.failure_mode: The deep ref flags Table 1.2's body as absent from the converted source, so the exclusion list cannot be verified; 'stakeholder mapping' does not appear anywhere in the source, and 'mind mapping' is described as a loose term that 'can refer to almost any of the methods in this book'
findings.fix: correct: It excludes other mapping methods listed in its Table 1.2 (not recoverable from the converted text) and broad schools of practice such as participatory action research

findings.claim: 'System Dynamics and Bayesian Belief Networks require quantitative data the team retro context rarely has'
findings.failure_mode: Source says the reverse for both: SD's founding figures held 'we did not need to revert to using highly quantitative factors with data to back them up'; BBNs have been built 'from data or from stakeholder input' from the start, and the authors recommend building a generic map with stakeholders
findings.fix: correct: System Dynamics and BBNs are more formal, slower to build and harder to start (SD 'requires a relatively large amount of time'; BBN elicitation 'can create rather repetitive conversations'), so this distillation focuses on Rich Pictures, CLDs, ToC and PSM

findings.claim: 'Rich Picture strengths ("flexibility, openness, ability to capture different perspectives") are [V] in the deep ref'; the process-value claim is restated 'without blockquoting'
findings.failure_mode: Wrong on both: the strengths list is deep-ref paraphrase, not [V]; Concept 8 does quote the process-value passage with [V]. The note also misses the unmarked quotations in Concepts 2, 6, 9
findings.fix: correct: rewrite the note to match what is quoted and marked after the D004-D008 fixes

notes: Integration rows for SSDL (five archetypes as hypothesis generators), Liberating Structures (TRIZ inversion) and Open Kanban (Holistic or Systemic Approach to Change, Deming + Goldratt) check out. The Gareth Morgan 15% note is accurate about Liberating Structures but irrelevant to this source. Recurring problems: (1) a Five Whys premise appears five times (lines 8, 20, 54, 75, 110) with no basis in the source; (2) Rich Pictures presented as a counter to dominant voices, which the source names as a Rich Pictures weakness to be handled only at planning and inviting; (3) the Ch 4 visual-literacy trick inverted into 'trim the map'. Most serious: D010/D018 (inverts the cited Ch 2 guidance), D013 (inverts the cited Ch 4 trick), D030 (SD/BBN data requirement the source denies).
